l: Moses' request to see God's glory, Exodus, Chapter 33
s: After the LORD agrees to go with them, Moses asks, "Please show me your glory." The LORD answers that he will make all his goodness pass before Moses and proclaim his name, being gracious and merciful to whom he chooses. He refuses to show his face, since no man can see it and live, but will place Moses in a cleft of the rock, cover him with his hand while his glory passes, and then let him see his back.

The LORD commands Moses to chisel two new stone tablets and come alone to Mount Sinai, where the LORD descends in a cloud and proclaims his name as merciful, gracious, and just. Moses bows and asks the LORD to go among the stiff-necked people and pardon them, and the LORD responds by making a covenant, promising marvels and the driving out of the Amorite, Canaanite, Hittite, Perizzite, Hivite, and Jebusite. Israel is commanded to make no covenant with the land's inhabitants, to destroy their altars, pillars, and Asherah poles, to make no cast idols, and to keep the feasts, the Sabbath, and the firstborn and offering laws. Moses spends forty days and nights with the LORD and writes the covenant words, the ten commandments, on the tablets. When he comes down, his face shines, the Israelites fear to approach, and he wears a veil except when speaking with the LORD.

The LORD orders new tablets made, descends in a cloud on Mount Sinai, and proclaims his name as merciful, gracious, slow to anger, abundant in loving kindness, forgiving, yet not clearing the guilty. He makes a covenant with Moses and Israel, promises marvels and the driving out of the land's peoples, and commands exclusive worship, since his name is Jealous.

Moses chisels two stone tablets, goes up Mount Sinai alone at the LORD's command, bows and worships, and intercedes for the stiff-necked people. After forty days and nights without food or water he writes the covenant words and comes down with a shining face, unaware of it, then veils his face except when speaking with the LORD.

Mount Sinai is where Moses is told to present himself on the top, with no one else and no flocks or herds nearby. The LORD descends there in a cloud, proclaims his name, and Moses stays forty days and nights before coming down with the tablets.

The LORD has Moses chisel two tablets like the first, which Moses broke, and promises to write on them the same words. Moses carries them up, writes the covenant words, the ten commandments, on them, and brings them down from Sinai.

The LORD makes a covenant, promising marvels before all the people and the driving out of the land's inhabitants, and tells Moses to write the words on which it rests with him and Israel. Its terms include no covenants with the inhabitants, no idols, and keeping the feasts, the Sabbath, and the firstborn laws. The words are written on the tablets as the ten commandments.

Israel is described as a stiff-necked people for whom Moses asks pardon and to be taken as the LORD's inheritance. They receive commands to destroy the idolatrous objects of the land, avoid covenants and intermarriage with its inhabitants, and keep the feasts and Sabbath. They fear Moses' shining face, then draw near to hear the commandments.

The LORD says he will drive out the Amorite, the Canaanite, the Hittite, the Perizzite, the Hivite, and the Jebusite before Israel. Israel is forbidden to make a covenant with them and must break down their altars, pillars, and Asherah poles, lest they become a snare leading Israel into idolatry.

Moses gathers the whole congregation of the children of Israel and relays the LORD's commands: observe the Sabbath as a day of solemn rest with no work or fire-kindling, and bring a willing offering of materials for the tabernacle and the priestly garments. He lists the materials and everything the wise-hearted are to make, from the ark and table to the altars, court hangings, and holy garments for Aaron and his sons. The people, men and women, return and bring gold jewelry, fabrics, skins, metals, wood, spices, oil, and stones, with the women spinning thread and the rulers bringing onyx and other stones. Moses then announces that the LORD has called Bezalel of Judah and Oholiab of Dan, filling them with wisdom and skill in all kinds of craftsmanship and the ability to teach.

Moses assembles the congregation and delivers the LORD's commands about the Sabbath, the offering, and the items to be made. He later announces that the LORD has called Bezalel and filled him and Oholiab with skill for the work.

The children of Israel are gathered and told to keep the Sabbath and to bring a willing offering. They respond, men and women alike, bringing jewelry, fabrics, skins, metals, wood, spices, oil, and stones as a free will offering for the work.

The LORD commands the Sabbath rest and calls for a willing offering and for wise-hearted workers to make the tabernacle, its furnishings, and the holy garments. He is said to have called Bezalel by name and filled him and Oholiab with the Spirit of God, wisdom, and skill.
The Sabbath is set out as the seventh day, a holy day of solemn rest to the LORD. Anyone who does work on it is to be put to death, and no fire is to be kindled in any habitation.

Bezalel, son of Uri, son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah, is announced as called by name by the LORD. He is filled with the Spirit of God, wisdom, understanding, knowledge, and all kinds of workmanship, including work in metals, stone cutting, and wood carving, and has it in his heart to teach.

Oholiab, son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan, is named alongside Bezalel as one who can teach. He is filled with wisdom of heart for all kinds of workmanship, including engraving, skilled work, embroidery, and weaving.

The tabernacle is to be made along with its covering, clasps, boards, bars, pillars, sockets, and pins. Its furnishings are also listed: the ark, mercy seat, table, lamp stand, incense altar, altar of burnt offering, basin, and court hangings.

l: offering (for the tabernacle work), Exodus, Chapter 35
s: The LORD commands an offering taken from the willing-hearted, consisting of metals, dyed and spun fabrics, skins, acacia wood, oil, spices, and stones. The people bring it freely, with the women spinning and the rulers bringing stones, spices, and oil, as a free will offering for the work.

Moses calls Bezalel, Oholiab, and every wise-hearted man whom the LORD has gifted with wisdom to do the work of the sanctuary according to the LORD's commands. The workers receive the Israelites' daily free will offerings from Moses until they report that the people have brought much more than enough, so Moses has a proclamation made that restrains the people from bringing more. The wise-hearted workers then make the tabernacle from ten curtains of fine linen with cherubim, joined by fifty blue loops and fifty gold clasps, plus eleven goats' hair curtains joined by bronze clasps, and coverings of rams' skins and sea cow hides. They also make the acacia boards with silver sockets for the south, north, and west sides, the bars with gold-covered rings, the veil with four gold-overlaid pillars on silver sockets, and the door screen with five pillars on bronze sockets.
Bezalel is named with Oholiab as one who shall work with every wise-hearted man, to whom the LORD has given wisdom and understanding for the sanctuary work. Moses calls him to the work.
Oholiab is named with Bezalel as one who shall work with every wise-hearted man in the service of the sanctuary according to all the LORD commanded. Moses calls him to the work.

Moses calls Bezalel, Oholiab, and the wise-hearted men to the work and gives them the offerings the Israelites brought. When the workers report there is more than enough, he commands a proclamation throughout the camp that no one make anything further for the offering, so the people are restrained from bringing.
The LORD is the one who put wisdom and understanding in Bezalel, Oholiab, and the wise-hearted men to do the sanctuary work. The work is made according to all that he commanded.

l: wise-hearted men (workers of the sanctuary), Exodus, Chapter 36
s: These men, whose hearts the LORD filled with wisdom and stirred to come, receive the offerings and tell Moses the people have brought more than enough. They then make the tabernacle curtains, coverings, boards, sockets, bars, veil, and door screen with its pillars.

The children of Israel bring offerings for the sanctuary work, continuing with free will offerings every morning. They bring so much that they are restrained by Moses' proclamation, since what they had was sufficient and too much.

The sanctuary is the object of the service for which the LORD gave the workers wisdom, and the offerings are brought for its work. The work on it is carried out according to all that the LORD commanded.

The tabernacle is made with ten linen curtains with cherubim, joined by loops and gold clasps so it is a unit. It is covered with goats' hair curtains, rams' skins dyed red, and sea cow hides, and is built with acacia boards on silver sockets, gold-covered bars, a veil, and a door screen.

l: offerings (for the sanctuary work), Exodus, Chapter 36
s: The offerings are received by the workers from Moses, and free will offerings keep coming every morning. They prove much more than enough, so Moses has the people stopped from bringing more, as the stuff was sufficient for all the work and too much.

Chapter 37 describes Bezalel's construction of the sacred furnishings. He makes the ark of acacia wood overlaid with gold, with rings and poles for carrying it, and a pure gold mercy seat with two beaten-work cherubim whose wings cover it. He then makes the table of acacia wood with its gold overlay, border, rings, poles, and gold vessels. He crafts the lamp stand of beaten pure gold with six branches, seven lamps, and accessories, made from a talent of gold. Finally he makes the acacia altar of incense overlaid with gold, along with the holy anointing oil and pure incense.

Bezalel is the craftsman who makes the ark, mercy seat, cherubim, table with its vessels, lamp stand, and altar of incense. He also makes the holy anointing oil and the pure incense of sweet spices, after the art of the perfumer.

l: ark of the covenant, Exodus, Chapter 37
s: Bezalel makes the ark of acacia wood, two and a half cubits long and a cubit and a half wide and high. He overlays it with pure gold inside and outside, adds a gold molding, casts four gold rings for its feet, and makes gold-overlaid acacia poles set in the rings to bear it.
Bezalel makes the mercy seat of pure gold, two and a half cubits long and a cubit and a half wide. The two cherubim are made of one piece with it at its two ends, and their wings cover it.

l: cherubim (on the mercy seat), Exodus, Chapter 37
s: Bezalel makes two cherubim of beaten gold, one at each end of the mercy seat and of one piece with it. They spread their wings above, covering the mercy seat, with their faces toward one another and toward the mercy seat.

Bezalel makes the table of acacia wood, two cubits long, a cubit wide, and a cubit and a half high, overlaid with pure gold with a gold molding. It has a hand's-width border with its own gold molding, four gold rings near the border for the carrying poles, and gold-overlaid acacia poles. He also makes its pure gold vessels: dishes, spoons, bowls, and pitchers for pouring out.

Bezalel makes the lamp stand of beaten pure gold, with its base, shaft, cups, buds, and flowers all of one piece. It has six branches, three on each side, with almond-blossom cups, and he adds seven lamps, snuffers, and snuff dishes of pure gold. The whole, with all its vessels, is made from a talent of pure gold.

Bezalel makes the altar of incense of acacia wood, square at a cubit by a cubit and two cubits high, with horns of one piece with it. He overlays its top, sides, and horns with pure gold, adds a gold molding, and makes two gold rings under the molding on its two sides for gold-overlaid acacia carrying poles.

Chapter 38 describes the construction of the bronze altar of burnt offering, with its horns, vessels, grating, rings, poles and bronze basin made from the mirrors of the ministering women. It then details the tabernacle court, with linen hangings, bronze sockets, silver hooks and fillets, pillars on each side, and an embroidered gate screen. Bezalel of Judah and Oholiab of Dan are named as the craftsmen who made everything the LORD commanded Moses. The chapter closes with an accounting, overseen by Ithamar son of Aaron, of the gold, the silver from the census of counted men, and the bronze, and how the silver and bronze were used for sockets, hooks, fillets, and other fittings.

l: altar of burnt offering, Exodus, Chapter 38
s: Made of acacia wood, square at five cubits by five cubits and three cubits high, with horns of one piece with it, all overlaid with bronze. It received bronze vessels, a bronze network grating, four rings, and acacia poles overlaid with bronze for carrying, and was made hollow with planks. Its sockets, grating and vessels were made from the offering bronze.

Enclosed by fine twined linen hangings: one hundred cubits on the south and north sides, fifty on the west and east, with twenty pillars and sockets per long side and ten on the west. Pillars stood on bronze sockets with silver hooks, fillets, and capital overlays, and the gate had a 20-cubit embroidered screen of blue, purple, scarlet, and linen on four pillars. The court's sockets and pins were made of bronze.

It is called the Tabernacle of the Testimony, and its materials were counted according to Moses' commandment for the Levites' service under Ithamar son of Aaron the priest. All its pins were of bronze, and Bezalel made everything the LORD commanded Moses.
Bezalel is identified as son of Uri, son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah. He made all that the LORD commanded Moses.
Oholiab, son of Ahisamach of the tribe of Dan, worked alongside Bezalel. He is described as an engraver, a skillful workman, and an embroiderer in blue, purple, scarlet, and fine linen.

l: gold of the offering, Exodus, Chapter 38
s: The gold used in all the work of the sanctuary, including the gold of the offering, totaled twenty-nine talents and seven hundred thirty shekels by the sanctuary shekel.

l: silver of the counted, Exodus, Chapter 38
s: Silver from those counted in the congregation came to one hundred talents and 1,775 shekels, at a beka (half shekel) a head from each man aged twenty and up, 603,550 men in all. The hundred talents were cast into one hundred sockets, one talent each, for the sanctuary and the veil, and the 1,775 shekels made hooks, capital overlays, and fillets for the pillars.

l: bronze of the offering, Exodus, Chapter 38
s: The bronze of the offering was seventy talents and 2,400 shekels. It was used for the sockets at the Tent of Meeting door, the bronze altar and its grating and vessels, the sockets around the court and its gate, and all the pins of the tabernacle and court.

Chapter 39 describes the Israelites making the priestly garments for Aaron and his sons exactly as the LORD commanded Moses. They craft the ephod with gold, blue, purple, scarlet and fine linen, with onyx stones engraved with the names of the children of Israel on its shoulder straps. They make the breastplate set with twelve stones for the twelve tribes and bind it to the ephod, then make the blue robe with bells and pomegranates, the linen tunics, turban, trousers and sash, and the gold plate inscribed "HOLY TO THE LORD". With all the work of the tabernacle finished, the people bring the tabernacle and all its furnishings and the garments to Moses, who sees that it was done as the LORD commanded and blesses them.

The LORD is the one whose commands to Moses govern every detail of the garments and the tabernacle work, a point repeated throughout the chapter. All the work is completed according to what he commanded.

Moses is the one to whom the LORD gave the commands that the workers follow. The children of Israel bring the finished tabernacle and its furnishings to him, he sees that the work was done as commanded, and he blesses them.

The children of Israel make the garments and all the tabernacle work according to all that the LORD commanded Moses. Their names are engraved on the onyx stones of the ephod and on the twelve stones of the breastplate, and they bring the finished work to Moses and receive his blessing.

The ephod is made of gold, blue, purple, scarlet and fine twined linen, with gold beaten into thin plates and cut into wires to be worked in. It has joined shoulder straps and a skillfully woven band of the same work, and onyx stones engraved with the names of the children of Israel are set on the shoulder straps as stones of memorial.

The breastplate is made square and double, a span by a span, in the same work as the ephod, and set with four rows of three stones in gold settings, one for each of the twelve tribes. It is attached by gold chains, gold rings and settings to the ephod's shoulder straps, and bound with a blue lace to the ephod's rings so that it stays on the woven band and does not come loose.

l: robe of the ephod, Exodus, Chapter 39
s: The robe of the ephod is made of woven work, all of blue, with a bound opening like that of a coat of mail so it will not tear. Its skirts have pomegranates of blue, purple, scarlet and twined linen alternating with pure gold bells, to minister in.

l: holy garments (for Aaron and his sons), Exodus, Chapter 39
s: The holy garments are made of blue, purple, scarlet and fine linen as finely worked garments for ministering in the holy place, including the tunics, turban, headbands, trousers and sash. A gold plate of the holy crown is inscribed "HOLY TO THE LORD" and tied to the turban with a blue lace. They are brought to Moses with the tabernacle work for the priest's office.

The work of the tabernacle of the Tent of Meeting is declared finished, having been done as the LORD commanded Moses. The children of Israel bring it to Moses with its tent, boards, furniture, altars, lamp stand, court hangings and instruments, and Moses sees it was done as commanded.

The LORD instructs Moses to raise up the tabernacle on the first day of the first month, arrange its furnishings, anoint it and its furniture, and wash, clothe, and anoint Aaron and his sons for an everlasting priesthood. Moses carries out every command: in the first month of the second year he sets up the tabernacle, places the ark, table, lamp stand, golden altar, altar of burnt offering, and basin, and raises the court. Once Moses finishes the work, the cloud covers the Tent of Meeting and the LORD's glory fills the tabernacle, so Moses cannot enter. The chapter closes by explaining that Israel journeyed onward only when the cloud lifted, and stayed put when it did not, with the cloud by day and fire in it by night.

The LORD commands Moses to raise up the tabernacle, arrange its furnishings, anoint everything, and consecrate Aaron and his sons as priests. After Moses finishes, the LORD's glory fills the tabernacle, and his cloud, with fire by night, guides Israel's journeys.

Moses receives the LORD's instructions and carries out each one exactly, raising the tabernacle, placing the ark and furnishings, offering sacrifices, and setting up the court. When the LORD's glory fills the tabernacle, he is unable to enter the Tent of Meeting.

The LORD commands that Aaron be brought to the door of the Tent of Meeting, washed, clothed in the holy garments, and anointed so he may minister in the priest's office. Aaron later washes his hands and feet at the basin with Moses and his sons.

Aaron's sons are to be brought to the door, washed, put in tunics, and anointed as their father was, to serve as priests. They wash their hands and feet at the basin, and again when entering the Tent or approaching the altar.

The tabernacle is raised on the first day of the first month of the second year, with its sockets, boards, bars, pillars, coverings, and roof, and furnished and surrounded by a court. Afterward the cloud covers it and the LORD's glory fills it.

l: ark of the covenant, Exodus, Chapter 40
s: Moses puts the covenant into the ark, sets the poles on it, places the mercy seat above it, and brings it into the tabernacle. He screens it with the veil, as the LORD commanded.
The LORD commands that Aaron and his sons be washed, clothed, and anointed to minister as priests. Their anointing is to give them an everlasting priesthood throughout their generations.

The cloud covers the Tent of Meeting once the work is finished, and stays on it so that Moses cannot enter. Its lifting signals Israel to travel, and it rests on the tabernacle by day with fire in it by night in sight of all Israel.

The children of Israel travel onward throughout all their journeys only when the cloud is taken up from the tabernacle, and do not move until the day it lifts. They see the cloud by day and the fire in it by night.

l: raising of the tabernacle, Exodus, Chapter 40
s: The LORD commands the raising of the tabernacle on the first day of the first month, and Moses does it on that day in the second year. He sets up each part and furnishing as commanded and finishes the work with the court and the gate screen.

In the wilderness of Sinai, on the first day of the second month of the second year after leaving Egypt, the LORD commands Moses and Aaron to count every male of the children of Israel aged twenty and upward who is able to go to war, by families and fathers' houses. A man who heads his fathers' house is named from each tribe to stand with them, and the census is carried out as commanded. The tribe-by-tribe totals are given, from Manasseh's thirty-two thousand two hundred to Judah's seventy-four thousand six hundred, and the whole count comes to six hundred three thousand five hundred fifty. The Levites are excluded from the count and appointed instead to care for, carry, take down, set up, and encamp around the Tabernacle of the Testimony, so that no wrath falls on the congregation. The other tribes are to camp each by their own standard, and the children of Israel do all that the LORD commanded.

The LORD speaks to Moses in the Tent of Meeting in the wilderness of Sinai and commands a census of the men able to go to war. He names the tribal heads who are to assist and orders that the Levites not be counted but be appointed over the Tabernacle, with the other tribes camping by their standards.

Moses receives the LORD's command to take the census, together with Aaron, and takes the named tribal leaders with him. He counts the people in the wilderness of Sinai as commanded, and he receives the instructions that exclude the Levites and assign them to the Tabernacle.
Aaron is told to count the men of Israel by their divisions together with Moses. He and Moses assemble the congregation, take the named leaders, and carry out the count.

The children of Israel are assembled on the first day of the second month and declare their ancestry by families and fathers' houses. They are counted tribe by tribe, totaling 603,550 men of fighting age, and are told to pitch their tents each by his own camp and standard. They do all that the LORD commanded.

The census counts every male twenty years old and upward able to go to war, by families and fathers' houses, tribe by tribe. The tribal totals are Reuben 46,500; Simeon 59,300; Gad 45,650; Judah 74,600; Issachar 54,400; Zebulun 57,400; Ephraim 40,500; Manasseh 32,200; Benjamin 35,400; Dan 62,700; Asher 41,500; Naphtali 53,400, for a total of 603,550. The tribe of Levi is excluded.

The tribe of Levi is not counted among the children of Israel in the census, by the LORD's command. The Levites are instead appointed over the Tabernacle of the Testimony and its furnishings, to carry it, care for it, take it down and set it up, and encamp around it.

l: princes (heads of the thousands of Israel), Numbers, Chapter 1
s: One man from each tribe, each head of his fathers' house, is named to stand with Moses and Aaron: Elizur of Reuben, Shelumiel of Simeon, Nahshon of Judah, Nethanel of Issachar, Eliab of Zebulun, Elishama of Ephraim, Gamaliel of Manasseh, Abidan of Benjamin, Ahiezer of Dan, Pagiel of Asher, Eliasaph of Gad, and Ahira of Naphtali. They are called the princes of the tribes and heads of the thousands of Israel, and they assist in the counting.

l: tabernacle (Tent of the Testimony), Numbers, Chapter 1
s: The Tabernacle of the Testimony is placed under the care of the Levites, who are to carry it and all its furnishings, take it down and set it up when it moves, and encamp around it. Any stranger who comes near it is to be put to death, and the Levites' encampment around it is meant to prevent wrath on the congregation.

The LORD instructs Moses and Aaron on how the children of Israel are to camp and travel around the Tent of Meeting, each man by his own standard and his fathers' house. Four camps of three tribes each are assigned to the east (Judah with Issachar and Zebulun), south (Reuben with Simeon and Gad), west (Ephraim with Manasseh and Benjamin), and north (Dan with Asher and Naphtali), each with a named prince and a counted total. The camps set out in the order Judah, Reuben, the Tent of Meeting with the Levites in the middle, Ephraim, and Dan last. The total counted of all the camps is 603,550, while the Levites are not counted among the children of Israel. The children of Israel do all that the LORD commanded Moses.
The LORD speaks to Moses and Aaron and gives the arrangement for how Israel is to encamp and set out by standards. He also commanded that the Levites not be counted among the children of Israel.
Moses, together with Aaron, receives the LORD's instructions on the encampment and marching order. The children of Israel carry out everything the LORD commanded Moses.

The children of Israel are told to encamp each man by his own standard around the Tent of Meeting at a distance from it. They are counted at 603,550 by their fathers' houses and obey, encamping and setting out by their standards, families, and fathers' houses.

The Tent of Meeting is the center around which all the tribes camp, at a distance from it. When the camps move, it sets out after the second camp, with the camp of the Levites in the middle of the camps.

The camp of Judah, with Issachar and Zebulun, encamps on the east side toward the sunrise under the prince Nahshon son of Amminadab. Its total is 186,400 (Judah 74,600, Issachar 54,400, Zebulun 57,400), and it sets out first.

The camp of Reuben, with Simeon and Gad, encamps on the south side, with Elizur son of Shedeur as prince of Reuben. Its total is 151,450 (Reuben 46,500, Simeon 59,300, Gad 45,650), and it sets out second.

The camp of Ephraim, with Manasseh and Benjamin, encamps on the west side, with Elishama son of Ammihud as prince of Ephraim. Its total is 108,100 (Ephraim 40,500, Manasseh 32,200, Benjamin 35,400), and it sets out third.

The camp of Dan, with Asher and Naphtali, encamps on the north side, with Ahiezer son of Ammishaddai as prince of Dan. Its total is 157,600 (Dan 62,700, Asher 41,500, Naphtali 53,400), and it sets out last.
The Levites encamp in the middle of the camps, and the Tent of Meeting sets out with them. They are not counted among the children of Israel, as the LORD commanded Moses.

l: census count of the tribes, Numbers, Chapter 2
s: Each tribe's division is given a count, from 32,200 for Manasseh to 74,600 for Judah. The camp totals are 186,400, 151,450, 108,100, and 157,600, and all counted of the camps came to 603,550, with the Levites excluded.

l: order of encampment and march, Numbers, Chapter 2
s: Judah is on the east, Reuben on the south, Ephraim on the west, and Dan on the north, around the Tent of Meeting. They march in the order Judah, Reuben, the Tent of Meeting with the Levites, Ephraim, and Dan last, and as they encamp, so they set out, each man in his place.

Chapter 3 lists the sons of Aaron (Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, Ithamar), noting that Nadab and Abihu died childless for offering strange fire. The LORD tells Moses to give the tribe of Levi to Aaron and his sons to serve the tabernacle, taking the Levites in place of Israel's firstborn, who are the LORD's because he struck down Egypt's firstborn. Moses counts the Levites by their three clans, Gershon, Kohath, and Merari, assigning each a camp position and tabernacle duties, for a total of twenty-two thousand males from a month old. Moses then counts Israel's firstborn males, finding twenty-two thousand two hundred seventy-three, and collects five shekels each for the two hundred seventy-three who exceed the Levites, a total of one thousand three hundred sixty-five shekels, which he gives to Aaron and his sons.

The LORD speaks to Moses at Sinai, commanding that the Levites be given to Aaron and his sons and be taken in place of all Israel's firstborn, who are his because he struck down Egypt's firstborn. He orders both censuses and sets the five-shekel redemption price for the surplus firstborn.

Moses carries out the LORD's commands by counting the Levites and then Israel's firstborn males. He collects the redemption money of one thousand three hundred sixty-five shekels and gives it to Aaron and his sons. He is also to camp east of the tabernacle with Aaron and his sons.

Aaron is the priest whose four sons are named, two of whom, Nadab and Abihu, died for offering strange fire and left no children. The Levites are given to him and his sons to serve, and he and his sons keep the priesthood, camp east of the tabernacle, and receive the redemption money.

The Levites are set before Aaron to minister to him and to keep the requirements of the congregation and the tabernacle. They are taken as the LORD's in place of Israel's firstborn, and twenty-two thousand males from a month old are counted in the three clans of Gershon, Kohath, and Merari.

The children of Israel are the people on whose behalf the Levites serve and whose firstborn are replaced by the Levites. Their firstborn males are counted, and the surplus is redeemed with money paid to Aaron and his sons.

The firstborn of Israel are the LORD's, made holy to him when he struck down Egypt's firstborn. Their males from a month old number twenty-two thousand two hundred seventy-three, and the Levites are taken in their place.

The Gershonites descend from Gershon through Libni and Shimei, forming the Libnite and Shimeite families, and number seven thousand five hundred males. They camp west behind the tabernacle under prince Eliasaph son of Lael, and are responsible for the tabernacle, tent, coverings, screens, court hangings, and cords.

The Kohathites descend from Kohath through Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel, and number eight thousand six hundred males. They camp on the south side under prince Elizaphan son of Uzziel, and are responsible for the ark, table, lamp stand, altars, sanctuary vessels, and screen, under Eleazar's oversight.

The Merarites descend from Merari through Mahli and Mushi, forming the Mahlite and Mushite families, and number six thousand two hundred males. They camp on the north side under prince Zuriel son of Abihail, and are responsible for the tabernacle's boards, bars, pillars, sockets, instruments, and the court pillars with their sockets, pins, and cords.

The tabernacle is served by the Levites, with each clan assigned particular parts to keep and camped around it: Gershonites west, Kohathites south, Merarites north, and Moses, Aaron, and his sons east. An outsider who comes near is to be put to death.

At the LORD's command Moses counts every Levite male from a month old and upward by fathers' houses and families. The clans total seven thousand five hundred Gershonites, eight thousand six hundred Kohathites, and six thousand two hundred Merarites, twenty-two thousand in all.

l: redemption of surplus firstborn, Numbers, Chapter 3
s: Because Israel's firstborn number two hundred seventy-three more than the Levites, the LORD commands five shekels each, by the sanctuary shekel of twenty gerahs, to redeem them. Moses collects one thousand three hundred sixty-five shekels and gives it to Aaron and his sons.

In Numbers 4, the LORD instructs Moses and Aaron to count the Levite clans of Kohath, Gershon, and Merari, aged thirty to fifty, who are eligible for service in the Tent of Meeting. The Kohathites are assigned to carry the most holy things after Aaron and his sons have covered them, and they must not touch or see them lest they die; Eleazar oversees the oil, incense, meal offering, and anointing oil. The Gershonites carry the curtains, coverings, screens, hangings, and cords under Ithamar, while the Merarites carry the boards, bars, pillars, sockets, pins, and cords, also under Ithamar. Moses, Aaron, and the princes count 2,750 Kohathites, 2,630 Gershonites, and 3,200 Merarites, totaling 8,580. Each man is counted and assigned according to his service and burden, as the LORD commanded Moses.

The LORD commands Moses and Aaron to count the Levite clans aged thirty to fifty and specifies the duties of each clan. He provides for the Kohathites' safety by having Aaron and his sons appoint each man's burden so that they do not die approaching the most holy things.

Moses receives the LORD's instructions for counting and assigning the Levite clans. With Aaron and the princes, he carries out the census and counts each man according to his service and burden, as the LORD commanded.

Aaron is addressed with Moses by the LORD and, with his sons, covers the sanctuary and its furnishings before the Kohathites carry them. He and his sons appoint each Kohathite to his service and burden, and the Gershonites' work is at the commandment of Aaron and his sons. He helps Moses count the Levites.

The Kohathites are assigned to carry the most holy things of the Tent of Meeting after Aaron and his sons have covered them, but they must not touch or see the sanctuary lest they die. They number 2,750 men aged thirty to fifty.

The Gershonites are assigned to carry the tabernacle curtains, coverings, screens, court hangings, cords, and related instruments, under the hand of Ithamar the son of Aaron. They number 2,630 men aged thirty to fifty.

The Merarites are assigned to carry the tabernacle's boards, bars, pillars, sockets, court pillars, pins, and cords, with their instruments assigned to them by name, under the hand of Ithamar. They number 3,200 men aged thirty to fifty.

The Levites are divided into the Kohathite, Gershonite, and Merarite clans, and those aged thirty to fifty who enter service are counted. The total is 8,580, each assigned according to his service and burden.

The Tent of Meeting is the place where the Levites aged thirty to fifty do their work. Its most holy things, curtains, boards, and furnishings are covered, carried, and cared for by the different Levite clans when the camp moves.

l: census of the Levites, Numbers, Chapter 4
s: The census counts Levite men aged thirty to fifty who enter service in the Tent of Meeting: 2,750 Kohathites, 2,630 Gershonites, and 3,200 Merarites. Moses, Aaron, and the princes carry it out according to the LORD's commandment, for a total of 8,580.

l: service and burden-bearing duties, Numbers, Chapter 4
s: Duties are divided by clan: the Kohathites carry the covered holy furnishings, the Gershonites the curtains and hangings, and the Merarites the structural frame parts. Eleazar oversees the oil, incense, and offerings, Ithamar oversees the Gershonites and Merarites, and each man is assigned his own burden.

In Numbers 5 the LORD gives Moses three commands for the children of Israel. First, lepers, those with discharges, and those unclean by a corpse, male and female, are to be put outside the camp so they do not defile the LORD's dwelling place, and the people do so. Second, anyone who trespasses against the LORD must confess, make full restitution plus a fifth, and give it to the wronged party or, if there is no kinsman, to the priest, along with a ram of atonement; holy gifts brought to the priest belong to him. Third, the law of jealousy provides that a husband who suspects his wife of unfaithfulness brings her to the priest, who sets her before the LORD with a barley meal offering and has her swear an oath and drink the water of bitterness; if guilty she will swell and her thigh fall away, and if innocent she will be free and conceive. The husband is free from iniquity, while the wife bears hers.

The LORD speaks to Moses three times, commanding the removal of the unclean from the camp, the rules for restitution of trespass, and the law of jealousy. He dwells in the midst of the camp, and the camp must not be defiled. In the jealousy ordeal the woman is set before him and he is invoked to bring the curse on her if she is guilty.
Moses receives the LORD's commands and is told to relay them to the children of Israel. He is the intermediary for the rules on the unclean, on restitution, and on the law of jealousy.
The children of Israel are commanded to put the unclean outside the camp, and they obey exactly as the LORD spoke to Moses. They are also given the rules for restitution and for the jealousy ordeal.
The camp is the place in the midst of which the LORD dwells, and it must not be defiled. Lepers, those with a discharge, and those unclean by a corpse, male and female, are put outside it.

l: unclean persons (lepers, those with discharge, those defiled by a corpse), Numbers, Chapter 5
s: These persons, both male and female, are ordered put outside the camp so they do not defile it. The children of Israel carry this out.

The priest receives restitution when the wronged party has no kinsman, along with the ram of atonement, and the holy things and heave offerings brought to him are his. In the jealousy ordeal he brings the woman before the LORD, prepares the holy water with dust from the tabernacle floor, looses her hair, administers the oath, writes the curses in a book and washes them into the water, waves the meal offering, burns a handful on the altar, and makes her drink the water.

The wife, whose husband suspects her of unfaithfulness whether or not she is actually defiled, is brought by him to the priest. She takes the oath, says "Amen, Amen," and drinks the water of bitterness. If guilty she will swell, her thigh will fall away, and she will be a curse among her people; if clean she will be free and conceive offspring. She bears her iniquity.

The husband, on whom the spirit of jealousy has come, brings his wife to the priest with her offering of barley meal. He sets her before the LORD for the priest to carry out the law. He is declared free from iniquity.

A man or woman who trespasses against the LORD must confess the sin and repay the guilt in full plus a fifth to the one wronged. If that person has no kinsman, the restitution goes to the LORD and belongs to the priest, in addition to the ram of atonement.

This law applies when a husband is jealous of his wife, whether or not she is defiled, and there is no witness. He sets her before the LORD, and the priest carries out the whole procedure on her. It leaves the husband free from iniquity and the wife to bear her own.

l: meal offering of jealousy, Numbers, Chapter 5
s: This is one tenth of an ephah of barley meal, with no oil or frankincense, described as a meal offering of memorial that brings iniquity to memory. The woman holds it, the priest waves it before the LORD, burns a handful on the altar as its memorial portion, and then gives her the water to drink.

This is holy water in an earthen vessel mixed with dust from the tabernacle floor, into which the priest wipes the written curses. The woman drinks it after the oath. If she is defiled it enters her and becomes bitter, making her body swell and her thigh fall away; if she is clean it does not harm her.

The priest has the woman swear this oath, declaring that if she has been defiled the LORD will make her a curse and an oath among her people, with her thigh falling away and her body swelling. The woman answers "Amen, Amen."

The LORD instructs Moses to tell the children of Israel the rules for a Nazirite vow, which a man or woman may take to separate themselves to the LORD. The Nazirite must abstain from wine, grape products, cutting the hair, and contact with dead bodies, even of close family. If someone dies suddenly nearby, the Nazirite is defiled and must shave the head, bring birds and a lamb as offerings, and restart the days of separation. When the vow period ends, the Nazirite brings a set of offerings to the Tent of Meeting, shaves the head and burns the hair, and may then drink wine. The LORD then tells Moses to have Aaron and his sons bless the children of Israel with a three-part blessing, putting his name on them.

The LORD speaks to Moses, giving the law of the Nazirite vow and the wording of the priestly blessing. He declares the Nazirite holy to him and says that when the priests put his name on the children of Israel, he will bless them.
Moses receives the LORD's instructions twice in this unit. He is told to speak to the children of Israel about the Nazirite vow and to speak to Aaron and his sons about how to bless the people.

The children of Israel are the audience for the Nazirite law, which allows any man or woman among them to take the vow. They are also the people to be blessed by Aaron and his sons, who put the LORD's name on them.

The Nazirite separates himself to the LORD, avoiding wine, grape products, razors, and dead bodies, and is holy throughout the days of separation. If defiled by a sudden death, he shaves his head, brings offerings, and loses the former days. At the end of the vow he brings offerings, shaves his head at the Tent of Meeting, burns the hair, and may then drink wine.

The Nazirite vow is a special vow, open to man or woman, of separation to the LORD for a set period. It requires abstaining from grape products, leaving the hair uncut, and avoiding the dead, and the person must do according to the vow made, in addition to what he can afford.
Aaron and his sons are told by the LORD, through Moses, to bless the children of Israel using a specific three-part formula.

The priest offers the sin offering and burnt offering to atone for a Nazirite defiled by a death. At the completion of the vow he presents the offerings, offers the ram and its meal and drink offerings, and waves the boiled shoulder, cake, and wafer, which are holy for the priest along with the breast and thigh.

Two turtledoves or young pigeons, one for a sin offering and one for a burnt offering, plus a male lamb as a trespass offering, are required when a Nazirite is defiled. At the end of the vow, the Nazirite brings a male lamb, an ewe lamb, a ram for peace offerings, unleavened bread, wafers, and meal and drink offerings.

The priestly blessing is the LORD's prescribed words for Aaron and his sons: that the LORD bless and keep, make his face shine and be gracious, and lift up his face and give peace. Speaking it puts the LORD's name on the children of Israel, and he promises to bless them.

On the day Moses finished setting up and anointing the tabernacle, its furniture, and the altar, the princes of Israel, heads of the tribes, brought six covered wagons and twelve oxen before the tabernacle. At the LORD's command Moses gave them to the Levites according to their service: two wagons and four oxen to the sons of Gershon, four wagons and eight oxen to the sons of Merari under Ithamar son of Aaron, and none to the sons of Kohath, who carried the sanctuary on their shoulders. The LORD directed that each prince offer on his own day for the altar's dedication, beginning with Nahshon son of Amminadab of Judah and continuing through twelve days to Ahira son of Enan of Naphtali. Each prince gave the identical offering of a silver platter, silver bowl, golden ladle, burnt, sin, and peace offerings, and the chapter totals them. It ends with Moses entering the Tent of Meeting and hearing the LORD's voice from above the mercy seat between the two cherubim.

Moses finished setting up and anointing the tabernacle and altar, then took the princes' wagons and oxen and gave them to the Levites as the LORD instructed. He received the LORD's command about the daily dedication offerings. At the end he entered the Tent of Meeting and heard the LORD speak to him from above the mercy seat between the two cherubim.

The LORD told Moses to accept the wagons and oxen and give them to the Levites according to their service. He also ordered that each prince offer on his own day for the altar's dedication. He spoke to Moses from above the mercy seat on the ark of the Testimony, from between the two cherubim.

l: princes (heads of the thousands of Israel), Numbers, Chapter 7
s: The princes, heads of their fathers' houses and over those who were counted, brought six covered wagons and twelve oxen, one wagon per two princes and one ox each. They then each gave an offering for the altar's dedication on successive days, in the same amounts, totaling twelve silver platters, twelve silver bowls, and twelve golden ladles with animals for sacrifice.
The tabernacle had just been set up, anointed, and sanctified by Moses along with all its furniture. The princes presented their wagons and oxen before it.

l: altar (dedicated by the princes), Numbers, Chapter 7
s: The altar had been anointed and sanctified with all its vessels. The twelve princes gave offerings for its dedication on the day it was anointed, each on his own appointed day before the altar.

The Levites received the wagons and oxen from Moses according to their service. The sons of Gershon got two wagons and four oxen, and the sons of Merari got four wagons and eight oxen under Ithamar son of Aaron. The sons of Kohath received none because they carried the sanctuary's holy things on their shoulders.

l: wagons and oxen (offering of the princes), Numbers, Chapter 7
s: The princes brought six covered wagons and twelve oxen before the tabernacle, a wagon for every two princes and an ox for each. The LORD told Moses to accept them for the service of the Tent of Meeting, and Moses distributed them to the Levites by their service.

Nahshon son of Amminadab, of the tribe of Judah, offered first, on the first day of the altar's dedication. His offering was a silver platter of 130 shekels and a silver bowl of 70 shekels full of flour and oil, a golden ladle of 10 shekels full of incense, and burnt, sin, and peace offering animals.

l: dedication offerings of the altar, Numbers, Chapter 7
s: Twelve princes each offered the same gifts on twelve successive days: a silver platter of 130 shekels, a silver bowl of 70 shekels, a golden ladle of 10 shekels, and animals for burnt, sin, and peace offerings. The totals were 2,400 shekels of silver, 120 shekels of gold, twelve bulls, twelve rams, and twelve lambs for burnt offering, twelve goats for sin offering, and twenty-four bulls, sixty rams, sixty goats, and sixty lambs for peace offerings.

The LORD instructs Moses to tell Aaron to light the seven lamps in front of the lamp stand, and Aaron does so; the lamp stand is described as beaten gold made according to the pattern the LORD showed Moses. The LORD then commands Moses to cleanse the Levites by sprinkling water, shaving, and washing clothes, and to offer bulls as a meal offering, sin offering, and burnt offering. The children of Israel lay hands on the Levites, and Aaron offers them as a wave offering so they may serve the LORD in place of the firstborn of Israel, whom the LORD sanctified when he struck Egypt's firstborn. Moses, Aaron, and the congregation carry out these commands, and the Levites then serve in the Tent of Meeting before Aaron and his sons. The LORD finally sets the Levites' service age from twenty-five years, with retirement at fifty, after which they assist their brothers but perform no service.

The LORD commands Moses about the lamps and about the cleansing and presentation of the Levites, declaring that he has taken them instead of the firstborn of Israel, whom he sanctified on the day he struck Egypt's firstborn. He gives the Levites as a gift to Aaron and his sons and sets their service age at twenty-five to fifty.
Moses receives the LORD's instructions about the lamps, the cleansing of the Levites, and their service terms. He, with Aaron and the congregation, carries out the commands concerning the Levites.

Aaron is told to light the seven lamps and does so as commanded. He offers the Levites as a wave offering before the LORD and makes atonement for them, and the Levites are given to him and his sons to serve.

The Levites are taken from among the children of Israel, cleansed, and offered as a wave offering, becoming the LORD's in place of the firstborn. They then serve in the Tent of Meeting before Aaron and his sons, working from age twenty-five and retiring from service at fifty, after which they assist their brothers.

The children of Israel lay their hands on the Levites and, with Moses and Aaron, do to them all the LORD commanded. Their firstborn, both man and animal, belong to the LORD, and the Levites are taken in place of them to serve and make atonement for Israel.

The Levites are presented before the Tent of Meeting, with the whole congregation assembled. After their cleansing, they go in to do their service there before Aaron and his sons, and the older Levites assist their brothers there after retirement.

l: cleansing of the Levites, Numbers, Chapter 8
s: The LORD commands that the Levites be cleansed by sprinkling water of cleansing, shaving their whole bodies, and washing their clothes, along with bull offerings. The Levites purify themselves and wash their clothes, and Aaron makes atonement for them, as the LORD commanded.

The Levites are to be offered as a wave offering before the LORD by Aaron, on behalf of the children of Israel, so that they may do the LORD's service. Aaron does this after the Levites are cleansed, setting them apart as the LORD's.

In the wilderness of Sinai, in the first month of the second year after leaving Egypt, the LORD tells Moses that the children of Israel are to keep the Passover at its appointed time, and they do so on the fourteenth day at evening. Certain men made unclean by a dead body could not keep it and ask Moses and Aaron why they are kept back, and Moses waits to hear from the LORD. The LORD answers by establishing a second-month Passover on the fourteenth day for those unclean or on a distant journey, warns that a clean man who is not traveling and fails to keep it will be cut off, and allows foreigners to keep it under the same statute. The chapter then describes how the cloud covered the tabernacle, appearing as fire at night, and how the children of Israel traveled or encamped according to whether the cloud lifted or remained, for any length of time, at the LORD's commandment by Moses.

The LORD speaks to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai, commanding that the Passover be kept in its appointed season. When the unclean men's question is brought to him, he establishes a second-month Passover for those unclean or on a distant journey, and extends the same statute to foreigners. He also directs Israel's traveling and encamping through the cloud, so that they move and rest at his commandment.

Moses receives the LORD's word and tells the children of Israel to keep the Passover. When the unclean men come before him and Aaron, he tells them to wait until he hears what the LORD will command, and then relays the LORD's provision for the second month. Israel's traveling and camping is described as the LORD's command given by Moses.

The children of Israel keep the Passover in the first month, on the fourteenth day at evening, in the wilderness of Sinai, as the LORD commanded Moses. They are told of the second-month provision and the penalty of being cut off for a clean, non-traveling man who neglects it. They travel or encamp according to the cloud, however long it stays, keeping the LORD's command.

The Passover is to be kept in its appointed season, on the fourteenth day of the first month at evening, according to all its statutes and ordinances, and Israel keeps it so in the wilderness of Sinai. The LORD adds that it may be kept in the second month with unleavened bread and bitter herbs, leaving none until morning and breaking no bone. A clean man not on a journey who fails to keep it is cut off and bears his sin, and a foreigner may keep it under the same statute.

l: unclean men (Israelites defiled by a dead body), Numbers, Chapter 9
s: Certain men, unclean because of the dead body of a man, could not keep the Passover on its day. They came before Moses and Aaron and asked why they were kept back from offering the LORD's offering in its season among the children of Israel. Their question leads the LORD to provide for a second-month Passover.

l: tabernacle (Tent of the Testimony), Numbers, Chapter 9
s: On the day the tabernacle was raised up, the cloud covered it, the Tent of the Testimony. It is the place over which the cloud rests, and the cloud's remaining on or being taken up from it determines whether Israel encamps or travels.

The cloud covers the tabernacle from the day it is raised, and at evening it has the appearance of fire until morning, continually. When it is taken up from over the Tent Israel travels, and where it remains Israel encamps. It stays sometimes a few days, sometimes one night, and sometimes two days, a month, or a year.

l: Israel's travel and encampment guided by the cloud, Numbers, Chapter 9
s: Israel travels when the cloud is taken up and encamps where it remains, doing both at the LORD's commandment. The length of each stay varies, from a night to many days, a month or a year, yet Israel remains encamped as long as the cloud stays and does not travel. This obedience is described as keeping the LORD's command by Moses.

The LORD establishes that anyone unclean by a dead body, or on a journey far away, in any generation, shall still keep the Passover in the second month on the fourteenth day at evening. They eat it with unleavened bread and bitter herbs, leave none until morning, and break no bone, following the full statute of the Passover. This provision answers the unclean men's complaint and is distinguished from the case of a clean man not on a journey, who is cut off if he fails to keep it.

In Numbers 10, the LORD instructs Moses to make two beaten silver trumpets to be blown by the sons of Aaron for assembling the congregation, directing the camps' journeys, going to war, and marking feasts and sacrifices. In the second year, second month, on the twentieth day, the cloud lifts from the tabernacle and Israel departs the wilderness of Sinai, with the tribes setting out in order under their named leaders, beginning with Judah and ending with Dan as rear guard. Moses urges Hobab, son of Reuel the Midianite, to come with them as their eyes in the wilderness, but Hobab says he will return to his own land and relatives. The ark of the LORD's covenant goes ahead three days' journey from the Mount of the LORD to seek a resting place, with the cloud over the people by day. Moses speaks a prayer whenever the ark sets out and whenever it rests.

The LORD speaks to Moses, commanding the making of two silver trumpets and setting out their uses as a statute forever, with the promise that Israel will be remembered before him and saved from enemies when they sound an alarm in war. He directs Israel's departure from Sinai by the lifting of the cloud and the commandment given through Moses. Moses cites him as having promised to give Israel the land and as having spoken good concerning Israel.

Moses receives the LORD's instructions for the two silver trumpets and their uses. He invites Hobab, his father-in-law, to journey with Israel, asking him to be their eyes in the wilderness and promising to share whatever good the LORD does for them. He speaks a prayer when the ark goes forward, asking the LORD to rise and scatter his enemies, and another when it rests, asking the LORD to return to the thousands of Israel.

l: silver trumpets (made by Moses), Numbers, Chapter 10
s: Two trumpets of beaten silver are to be made, to be used for calling the congregation and for the journeying of the camps. Blowing both gathers all the congregation at the door of the Tent of Meeting, blowing one gathers the princes, and an alarm sends the east camps and then the south camps forward. They are also to be sounded as an alarm in war and blown over burnt offerings and peace offerings on days of gladness, set feasts, and the beginnings of months as a memorial before God.

Israel is instructed in the trumpet signals and then departs the wilderness of Sinai in the second year, tribe by tribe under named army leaders, in the order Judah, Reuben, Ephraim, and Dan. They travel toward the place the LORD said he would give them. They set out from the Mount of the LORD with the ark going before them three days' journey, and they are covered by the cloud by day.
The sons of Aaron, the priests, are appointed to blow the trumpets. This is established as a statute forever throughout Israel's generations.

The cloud is taken up from over the tabernacle of the covenant on the twentieth day of the second month of the second year, the signal for Israel to set out. It then stays in the wilderness of Paran. It is over the people by day when they set forward from the camp.

l: tabernacle (Tent of the Testimony), Numbers, Chapter 10
s: The cloud is lifted from over the tabernacle of the covenant, marking the start of Israel's journey. The tabernacle is taken down and carried by the sons of Gershon and the sons of Merari, while the Kohathites carry the sanctuary. The others set up the tabernacle before the Kohathites arrive.

Hobab is identified as the son of Reuel the Midianite and Moses' father-in-law. Moses invites him to come with Israel, but he refuses, saying he will go to his own land and relatives. Moses asks again, saying Hobab knows how to encamp in the wilderness and can be their eyes, and promises him the same good the LORD does for Israel.

l: ark of the LORD’s covenant, Numbers, Chapter 10
s: The ark goes before Israel three days' journey from the Mount of the LORD to seek out a resting place for them. When it goes forward, Moses calls on the LORD to rise and scatter his enemies, and when it rests, he asks the LORD to return to the thousands of Israel.

l: Israel's journey from Sinai, Numbers, Chapter 10
s: The journey begins in the second year, second month, on the twentieth day, when the cloud lifts, and Israel leaves the wilderness of Sinai according to the LORD's commandment by Moses. The tribes march in order: Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun first, then the Gershonites and Merarites with the tabernacle, then Reuben, Simeon, and Gad, the Kohathites with the sanctuary, Ephraim, Manasseh, and Benjamin, and finally Dan, Asher, and Naphtali as rear guard. The ark leads them three days' journey from the Mount of the LORD.

In Numbers 11 the people of Israel complain, and the LORD's fire burns the outskirts of the camp until Moses prays; the place is named Taberah. The mixed multitude and the Israelites then crave meat, longing for the food of Egypt and disdaining the manna. Moses, overwhelmed, tells the LORD the burden is too heavy and asks to die, so the LORD has him gather seventy elders and puts some of the Spirit on Moses onto them, and they prophesy. Eldad and Medad prophesy in the camp, Joshua asks Moses to forbid them, and Moses says he wishes all the LORD's people were prophets. The LORD sends a wind that brings quails, but while the people are still eating, he strikes them with a plague, and the place is named Kibroth Hattaavah before the people move on to Hazeroth.

The LORD burns the camp's outskirts with fire at the people's complaining, then promises meat for a month until it is loathsome, and asks whether his hand has grown short. He takes some of the Spirit on Moses and puts it on the seventy elders, sends a wind that brings quails, and strikes the people with a great plague while the meat is still between their teeth.

Moses prays and the fire abates, then tells the LORD that the burden of the people is too heavy and asks to be killed rather than see his wretchedness. He gathers the seventy elders, doubts how enough meat could be found for 600,000 men on foot, and answers Joshua's demand by wishing that all the LORD's people were prophets.

The people complain and weep for meat, remembering the fish, cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions and garlic of Egypt and scorning the manna. The LORD's fire burns among them at Taberah, and after they gather quails greedily, a great plague strikes them and they bury those who lusted at Kibroth Hattaavah before traveling to Hazeroth.

The manna is described as like coriander seed and looking like bdellium. The people ground, beat, boiled and made cakes of it, and it tasted like fresh oil. It fell on the camp with the dew at night, yet the people complain that there is nothing but manna to look at.

The people crave meat, and the LORD promises to give it to them for a whole month until it comes out of their nostrils and is loathsome. Moses doubts that flocks, herds or all the fish of the sea could supply it. The meat is provided as quails, and the LORD strikes the people with a plague while it is still between their teeth.

A wind from the LORD brings quails from the sea and drops them around the camp, about a day's journey in each direction and about two cubits above the ground. The people gather them for a day, a night and another day, with the least gatherer collecting ten homers, and spread them out around the camp.

Seventy elders of Israel, known as elders and officers over the people, are gathered by Moses at the Tent of Meeting so they can share the burden of the people. The LORD puts some of the Spirit that was on Moses onto them, and they prophesy but do not do so again.
Eldad stays in the camp rather than going out to the Tent, although he is among those who were written. The Spirit rests on him and he prophesies in the camp, which a young man reports to Moses.

Medad, like Eldad, remains in the camp and does not go out to the Tent, though he is among those who were written. The Spirit rests on him and he prophesies in the camp, prompting Joshua to ask Moses to forbid them.

The LORD takes some of the Spirit that is on Moses and puts it on the seventy elders, and they prophesy when it rests on them. The Spirit also rests on Eldad and Medad in the camp, and Moses wishes the LORD would put his Spirit on all his people.

Miriam and Aaron speak against Moses because of the Cushite woman he had married, asking whether the LORD has spoken only through Moses. The LORD hears them, summons all three to the Tent of Meeting, and declares that Moses is faithful in all his house and is spoken to mouth to mouth, unlike other prophets. The LORD's anger burns against Miriam and Aaron, and Miriam becomes leprous, as white as snow. Aaron confesses their foolish sin to Moses, and Moses cries to the LORD to heal her. The LORD orders Miriam shut outside the camp for seven days, and the people do not travel until she is brought back, after which they move from Hazeroth to the wilderness of Paran.

Miriam, with Aaron, spoke against Moses over the Cushite woman he had married and questioned whether the LORD had spoken only with him. She was rebuked at the Tent of Meeting and then became leprous, as white as snow. She was shut outside the camp for seven days and the people waited until she was brought in again.

Aaron joined Miriam in speaking against Moses and was called with her to the Tent of Meeting, where the LORD rebuked them both. After seeing Miriam leprous, he addressed Moses as "my lord," asked that the sin not be counted against them, and confessed that they had acted foolishly and sinned.

Moses is described as very humble, more than all men on the surface of the earth. The LORD declares him a faithful servant in all his house, one with whom he speaks mouth to mouth, plainly, and who sees the LORD's form. When Miriam became leprous, Moses cried to the LORD to heal her.

The LORD heard Miriam and Aaron's complaint, summoned them with Moses to the Tent of Meeting, and came down in a pillar of cloud. He explained that he speaks to prophets in visions and dreams but to Moses plainly, mouth to mouth. His anger burned against Miriam and Aaron, and he departed, after which Miriam was leprous. He answered Moses' plea by ordering her shut outside the camp for seven days and then brought in again.

Miriam's leprosy appeared, as white as snow, when the cloud departed from over the Tent after the LORD's anger burned against her and Aaron. Aaron begged that she not be as one dead, and Moses asked for her healing. The LORD set a term of seven days shut outside the camp, after which she would be brought in again.

l: Miriam and Aaron's sin against Moses, Numbers, Chapter 12
s: Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses because of his Cushite wife and asked whether the LORD had spoken only with him. The LORD heard it, rebuked them for not fearing to speak against his servant, and his anger burned against them. Aaron later acknowledged it as a foolish sin, and Miriam was struck with leprosy and shut outside the camp for seven days.

The LORD instructs Moses to send one leader from each tribe to spy out the land of Canaan, and Moses sends twelve named men from the wilderness of Paran, renaming Hoshea son of Nun as Joshua. Moses tells them to observe the land, its people, cities, and fertility, and to bring back fruit. The spies travel from the wilderness of Zin to Rehob and Hebron, cut a huge cluster of grapes at the valley of Eshcol, and return after forty days to Moses, Aaron, and the congregation at Kadesh. They report that the land flows with milk and honey but that its people are strong, its cities fortified, and the children of Anak live there. Caleb urges immediate conquest, but the other spies give an evil report, claiming the land devours its inhabitants and that they felt like grasshoppers beside the Nephilim.
The LORD speaks to Moses and commands him to send a prince from each tribe to spy out the land of Canaan, which He says He gives to the children of Israel.

Moses sends twelve tribal leaders from the wilderness of Paran to spy out Canaan, following the LORD's commandment, and gives them detailed instructions about what to observe and to bring back fruit. He also calls Hoshea son of Nun Joshua, and receives the spies' report at Kadesh.

Twelve men, one prince from each tribe, are sent to explore Canaan from Zin to Rehob and Hebron, and they return after forty days with fruit and a report. They agree the land is rich but ten of them, those who went up with Caleb, declare the people too strong to attack and spread an evil report.

l: Caleb the son of Jephunneh, Numbers, Chapter 13
s: Caleb son of Jephunneh of the tribe of Judah is one of the twelve spies. After the report, he stills the people before Moses and urges them to go up at once and possess the land, saying they are well able to overcome it.
Hoshea son of Nun, of the tribe of Ephraim, is among the twelve spies. Moses called him Joshua.

The children of Israel are the people to whom the land is promised, and each of their tribes supplies a spy. At Kadesh the congregation is shown the fruit and hears both Caleb's call to conquer and the other spies' evil report.

Canaan is the land the LORD gives to the Israelites, described by the spies as flowing with milk and honey. Its inhabitants include Amalek in the South, the Hittite, Jebusite, and Amorite in the hill country, and the Canaanite by the sea and along the Jordan, with fortified, very large cities.

The spies come to the valley of Eshcol and cut down a branch with one cluster of grapes, carried on a staff between two men, along with pomegranates and figs. The place is named Eshcol because of the cluster the Israelites cut down there.

Ahiman, Sheshai, and Talmai, children of Anak, are at Hebron when the spies arrive. The spies later cite the children of Anak as evidence of the land's strength, calling them Nephilim and men of great stature.

The expedition goes up by the South into the hill country, passing from the wilderness of Zin to Rehob near Hamath, and through Hebron and Eshcol. It lasts forty days and ends with the return to Kadesh, where the spies report to Moses, Aaron, and the congregation.
A branch bearing one cluster of grapes is cut at the valley of Eshcol and carried on a staff between two men. It is shown to the congregation as fruit of the land and gives the valley its name.

The men who went up with Caleb bring an evil report to the Israelites, saying they cannot go up against the stronger people and that the land eats up its inhabitants. They add that the people are of great stature, including the Nephilim, and that the spies seemed like grasshoppers in their own sight and in the sight of those people.

After the spies' report, the whole congregation of the children of Israel weeps and murmurs against Moses and Aaron, wishing to die in Egypt or choose a leader to return there. Joshua and Caleb tear their clothes and urge the people not to rebel or fear the people of the land, but the congregation threatens to stone them. The LORD threatens to strike the people with pestilence, but Moses intercedes by appealing to the LORD's reputation and his own words about loving kindness, and the LORD pardons yet decrees that the adult generation will die in the wilderness over forty years, sparing only Caleb and Joshua. The spies who brought the evil report die by plague, and when the people then presume to go up the mountain against Moses' warning, the Amalekites and Canaanites defeat them as far as Hormah.

The LORD appears in glory at the Tent of Meeting, threatens to strike the people with pestilence and disinherit them, then pardons them at Moses' plea. He nonetheless decrees that the adults who complained will die in the wilderness over forty years, brings in their little ones, and promises Caleb entry to the land. He is not with the people when they presume to go up the mountain, and they are defeated.

Moses and Aaron fall on their faces before the assembly when the people murmur. Moses intercedes for the people, arguing that the Egyptians and nations would say the LORD was unable to bring them in, and cites the LORD's slowness to anger and abundant loving kindness. He relays the sentence to the people and warns them not to go up the mountain, and he stays in the camp with the ark.

Joshua, one of those who spied out the land, tears his clothes and with Caleb tells the congregation the land is exceedingly good and not to rebel or fear. The people threaten to stone them. He is named as one of only two adults, with Caleb, who will enter the land, and he remains alive when the other spies die.

l: Caleb the son of Jephunneh, Numbers, Chapter 14
s: Caleb, a spy, tears his clothes and with Joshua urges the people to trust the LORD and not fear the people of the land. The LORD calls him his servant, says he had another spirit and followed fully, and promises to bring him into the land he entered, with his offspring possessing it. He survives while the other spies die by plague.

The children of Israel weep, murmur against Moses and Aaron, wish they had died in Egypt or the wilderness, and propose choosing a leader to return to Egypt. They threaten to stone Joshua and Caleb, then are sentenced to wander forty years. After mourning, they presume to go up the mountain against Moses' warning and are beaten down to Hormah.

Egypt is the place the people wish they had died in and want to return to under a new leader. Moses says the Egyptians would hear of it if the LORD killed the people he brought out by his might. The LORD's signs were worked there.

The land is described by Joshua and Caleb as exceedingly good and flowing with milk and honey, and the LORD swore it to the fathers. The people reject it, so that generation of adults, except Caleb and Joshua, will not see it. Their little ones will be brought in to know it.

The people wish they had died in the wilderness, and the LORD decrees that their dead bodies will fall and be consumed there. Their children will wander in it forty years, and the people are told to turn toward it by the way to the Red Sea. The LORD's signs were also worked in the wilderness.

The Amalekite is said to dwell in the valley, which is why the LORD tells the people to turn toward the wilderness. Moses warns that the Amalekite and Canaanite are before them. The Amalekites come down and strike the presumptuous Israelites, beating them to Hormah.

The Canaanite dwells in the valley along with the Amalekite, and Moses warns the people they will fall by the sword before them. The Canaanites who lived in that mountain come down with the Amalekites and beat the Israelites down to Hormah.

The men Moses sent to spy out the land return with an evil report that makes the congregation murmur against him. Those who brought the evil report die by plague before the LORD. Only Joshua and Caleb remain alive of the spies.

l: Israelites' rebellion and punishment of forty years, Numbers, Chapter 14
s: The congregation's complaining, refusal to enter the land, and tempting of the LORD ten times lead to the sentence that all counted adults from twenty years old and upward will die in the wilderness, except Caleb and Joshua. Their children will wander forty years, one year for each of the forty days of spying, bearing the people's iniquities. Their attempt to go up afterward without the LORD fails in defeat.

In Numbers 15 the LORD gives Moses instructions for the children of Israel about life in the land they will enter. He specifies the meal and drink offerings that accompany lambs, rams, and bulls offered by fire, and declares one law for native-born Israelites and for the foreigner living among them. He commands a wave offering from the first of their dough, and provides sacrifices and atonement for unwitting sins, while the one who sins with a high hand is to be cut off. A man found gathering sticks on the Sabbath is held in custody, then stoned outside the camp by the whole congregation at the LORD's command. The chapter ends with the command to make fringes with a blue cord on garment borders so the people will remember and do all the LORD's commandments.

The LORD speaks to Moses four times, giving instructions on offerings, the dough offering, unwitting sin, and fringes. He commands that the Sabbath breaker be put to death by stoning, and identifies himself as the God who brought Israel out of Egypt.

Moses receives the LORD's words and is told to relay them to the children of Israel. The congregation brings the stick-gatherer to him and Aaron, and he receives the LORD's judgment on the man, which the people carry out as the LORD commanded him.

The children of Israel are told what to offer once they enter the land, including the first of their dough as a wave offering. They are given provisions for unwitting sin, and as a congregation they stone the Sabbath breaker outside the camp. They are also told to wear fringes with a blue cord to remember the LORD's commandments and to be holy to their God.

l: stranger (foreigner living among Israel), Numbers, Chapter 15
s: The stranger who lives as a foreigner among Israel is to offer offerings by fire just as the native-born do, under one statute, one law, and one ordinance forever. The stranger is also forgiven along with the congregation for unwitting sin, and a foreigner who sins with a high hand is cut off like a native-born person.

l: offerings by fire (burnt offerings, sacrifices), Numbers, Chapter 15
s: Offerings of the herd or flock, made as burnt offerings, sacrifices, vows, free will offerings, or at set feasts, must be accompanied by fine flour mixed with oil and a wine drink offering. The amounts scale by animal: one tenth of an ephah of flour with a fourth of a hin of oil and wine for a lamb, two tenths with a third of a hin for a ram, and three tenths with half a hin for a bull. They are described as a pleasant aroma to the LORD.

l: unwitting sin and atonement, Numbers, Chapter 15
s: If the whole congregation errs unwittingly, it offers a young bull as a burnt offering with its meal and drink offerings, plus a male goat as a sin offering, and the priest makes atonement so they are forgiven. An individual who sins unwittingly offers a female goat a year old and is likewise forgiven, while one who acts with a high hand despises the LORD's word and is utterly cut off.

A man is found gathering sticks on the Sabbath while Israel is in the wilderness. Those who found him bring him to Moses, Aaron, and the congregation, and he is held in custody because no penalty had yet been declared.

l: stoning of the Sabbath breaker, Numbers, Chapter 15
s: The LORD declares that the man shall surely be put to death by the whole congregation stoning him outside the camp. The congregation brings him out and stones him to death, as the LORD commanded Moses.

l: fringes with blue cord, Numbers, Chapter 15
s: The LORD commands the Israelites to make fringes on the borders of their garments throughout their generations, with a blue cord on each border. The fringe is to be seen so they remember and do all the LORD's commandments, and do not follow their own hearts and eyes, and so that they may be holy to their God.

The LORD's commandments given through Moses are to be observed from the day they were given and throughout the generations, and failure to observe them unwittingly requires sin offerings. Deliberately breaking his commandment with a high hand brings being cut off, and the fringes are given so the people will remember and do all of them.

Korah, a Levite, joins Dathan, Abiram, and On of Reuben and 250 princes of the congregation in challenging Moses and Aaron, claiming all the congregation is holy. Moses proposes a test with censers before the LORD, while Dathan and Abiram refuse to come and accuse him of leading them out of a land flowing with milk and honey to die in the wilderness. When Moses warns the people to move away from the rebels' tents, the ground splits and swallows Korah, Dathan, Abiram, and their households alive into Sheol, and fire from the LORD consumes the 250 men offering incense. Eleazar hammers the rebels' bronze censers into a covering for the altar as a memorial that no outsider to Aaron's offspring should burn incense. The next day the congregation complains that Moses and Aaron killed the LORD's people, and a plague kills 14,700 until Aaron, at Moses' direction, runs among them with incense and makes atonement.

Korah, son of Izhar and a descendant of Levi, leads a challenge against Moses and Aaron, saying the whole congregation is holy. Moses rebukes him for seeking the priesthood in addition to his Levite service. Korah assembles the congregation at the Tent of Meeting and is swallowed alive by the earth with his household and goods.

Moses falls on his face when challenged, then proposes a censer test to show whom the LORD chooses, and he rebukes Korah and the Levites. He asks the LORD not to respect the rebels' offering, warns the congregation to leave the rebels' tents, and declares that the ground opening would prove the LORD sent him. When the congregation later blames him and Aaron, he directs Aaron to make atonement with incense to stop the plague.
